title: Petra and the Parish
premise: Vesper Ishikawa's quiet retirement shatters when two letters arrive: one confessing to the death of Father Anselm thirty years ago, the other promising a fourth death unless Vesper stops asking questions. As Vesper reopens the old case, they discover the parish's beloved vicar was poisoned by someone protecting an inheritance meant for the church—and that the confessor and the threatener are two different people. The trail leads to a dying parishioner whose will names Vesper's late partner as a beneficiary. In the end, Vesper must choose between exposing the killer, who is the last living link to the partner they loved, or letting the truth stay buried to protect a grieving family.
about_author: Emrys Kavanagh is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confessional letters in rural England before turning to fiction. Their debut novel draws on the quiet, complicit silences of small communities they observed firsthand.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Hand
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. In their failing bookshop, Vesper opens two letters in the same handwriting: a confession to Father Anselm's poisoning, and a threat promising a fourth death. The emotional beat is dread wrapped in reluctant excitement—the old detective instinct stirring after years of deliberate invisibility. Vesper burns neither letter and tells no one, beginning to investigate alone.

chapters.title: The Alibi of Thirty Years
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Reinterviewing aging parishioners, Vesper finds every suspect's alibi hinges on the same choir practice—a perfect, rehearsed cover. A hymnal margin note reveals Anselm had discovered a forged will redirecting the Merrow inheritance. Emotional beat: mounting unease as Vesper realizes the conspiracy is communal, and that their late partner, Daniel, was the solicitor who notarized the forgery.

chapters.title: What the Confession Withheld
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, with a flashback interlude in Daniel's voice. Vesper confronts the letter-writer: Margaret Merrow, who confessed to shield her son, the true poisoner. But the threatening letter arrives again—someone else knows. The climax breaks in the church crypt where Margaret's son, dying of the same illness that killed Anselm's first victim, tries to silence Vesper. Emotional beat: love against duty as Vesper recognizes Daniel's handwriting on the forged will.

chapters.title: The Fourth Death
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The fourth death is Margaret's own—she drank the poison meant for Vesper, dying with the truth half-told. Vesper must decide: hand the son to the police or honor the confession's plea. Choosing truth over loyalty, Vesper testifies, then closes the bookshop and leaves town, mailing one final letter—to the police, confessing the three earlier cases they solved and never reported. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into hard-won peace.
